edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Felix sacramentum aquae nostrae qua abluti delictis pristinae caecitatis, in vitam aeternam liberamur. Non erit otiosum digestum istud, instruens tam eos qui cum maxime formantur, quam et illos qui simpliciter credidisse contenti, non exploratis rationibus traditionum, intentatam probabilem fidem per imperitiam portant: atque adeo nuper conversata istic quaedam de Caiana haeresi vipera venenatissima doctrina sua plerosque rapuit, imprimis Baptismum destruens. Plane secundum naturam: nam fere viperae, et aspides, ipsique reguli serpentes arida et inaquosa sectantur. Sed nos pisciculi secundum ΙΧΘΥΝ nostrum Jesum Christum in qua nascimur, nec aliter quam in aqua permanendo salvi sumus. Ita Quintillia monstrosissima, cui nec integre quidem docendi jus erat, optime norat pisciculos necare, de aqua auferens.
pass_a_gloss: The sacrament of our water is happy by which having been washed we are freed from the offenses of former blindness into eternal life. This digest will not be idle, teaching both those who are being formed to the maximum degree and also those who are content to have believed simply, not having explored the reasons of traditions, they carry probable faith attempted through ignorance: and so recently a certain viper of the Caian heresy with its most poisonous doctrine seized many, especially destroying Baptism. Clearly according to nature: for nearly all vipers and asps and even the king snakes follow dry and waterless places. But we little fish according to our ΙΧΘΥΝ Jesus Christ in which we are born, and we are saved not otherwise than by remaining in water. Thus Quintilla most monstrous, who did not even have the right to teach wholeheartedly, knew very well to kill little fish, taking them away from the water.

choices.why: sacramentum can be translated to sacrament and felix to happy

choices.english: by which having been washed we are freed from the offenses
rejected: through which we are washed clean of sins
choices.why: literal translation of the Latin phrase
ΙΧΘΥΝ is the Greek word for fish and should be transliterated as is
pisciculi is the diminutive form of piscis, meaning little fish
literal translation of the Latin phrase

pass_b_english: Our water's sacrament is a blessed thing: washed in it, we are set free from the sins of our former blindness into eternal life. This digest will not be wasted effort. It instructs both those who are being most thoroughly formed and those who are merely content to have believed simply, without exploring the reasons behind the traditions, who carry an untested, probable faith through sheer ignorance. And so, recently a certain viper of the Caian heresy seized many with its most poisonous doctrine, destroying Baptism above all. Naturally enough: for vipers, asps, and even king snakes all seek out dry and waterless places. But we are little fish, born in our ΙΧΘΥΣ, Jesus Christ; we are saved only by remaining in water. Thus that most monstrous Quintilla, who did not even have the right to teach properly, knew perfectly well how to kill little fish: by dragging them out of the water.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The Greek term ΙΧΘΥΝ is correctly handled as a transliteration/reference to the Christological symbol. The translation of 'Quintilla' and the description of her teaching rights match the Latin 'cui nec integre quidem docendi jus erat'.
